#1
L: Fearlessness, purity-of-being, steadfastness-in-the-yoga-of-knowledge; giving, and self-control, and sacrifice, and study, austerity, uprightness;
I: Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge; giving, self-control, sacrifice, study of scripture, austerity, uprightness;
N: With no question from Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa continues directly (the speaker line at the head of this verse is generated separately; see conventions.md). Verses 1-3 are a single long asyndetic list of divine qualities — nouns simply set side by side with almost no ca, 'and' — and the sentence's only finite verb, bhavanti, 'they become, they constitute', does not arrive until the end of verse 3. Sandhi: token 2 hides two separate words fused together, sattvasaṃśuddhiḥ + jñānayogavyavasthitiḥ (-iḥ+j-→-ir j-) — 'purity of being' and 'steadfastness in the discipline (yoga, kept untranslated per convention) of knowledge'. In line 2, damaśca and yajñaśca both show -aḥ+c-→-aś c-, a pattern that recurs constantly through this chapter's lists. Svādhyāyastapa āra rjavam is unusual: after svādhyāyaḥ tapaḥ (-aḥ+t-→-as t-), tapaḥ's own visarga simply drops before ārjavam's vowel with the hiatus kept rather than the vowels fusing to tapārjavam — an accepted option in epic verse already seen at 15.16's akṣaraḥ eva.
#2
L: Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom-from-anger, renunciation, tranquility, and freedom-from-malice; compassion toward-beings, freedom-from-greed, gentleness, modesty, freedom-from-fickleness;
I: Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, avoidance of malice; compassion for living beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, a sense of shame, steadiness of mind;
N: The list continues. Token 2, satyam akrodhas tyāgaḥ, hides three separate words (satyam simply joined to akrodhaḥ before the vowel; akrodhaḥ+tyāgaḥ, -aḥ+t-→-as t-). Several items here are themselves privative a- formations, each treated as a single hyphenated lemma (a-krodha, a-paiśuna, a-lolupa-tva, a-cāpala) rather than split into separate morphs, following the pattern already set for such words at 15.5 and 15.7 (a-vyaya, a-mūḍha, a-cetas). Dayā bhūteṣu, 'compassion toward beings', is the one item in the list that governs a case (locative) rather than standing alone.
#3
L: Vigor, patience, fortitude, cleanliness, freedom-from-malice, and freedom-from-excessive-pride — these come-to-be the divine endowment of one born [to it], O Bhārata.
I: vigor, patience, fortitude, cleanliness, freedom from malice, and freedom from excessive pride — these, Bhārata, belong to one born with the divine endowment.
N: This closes the sentence begun at verse 1: bhavanti, 'they become', governs the whole three-verse list as its subject and takes sampadam daivīm, 'the divine endowment', as an accusative of the result reached rather than an ordinary nominative predicate — the traditional (Śaṅkara) sense is 'these [qualities] redound to, constitute, the divine endowment of one born [with such a nature]', abhijātasya being a genitive agreeing with an understood 'person'. Nātimānitā, 'freedom from excessive pride' (na+atimānitā, a+a→ā), closes the divine list on a quality that verse 4's darpa, 'pride', will directly oppose in the demonic list — one of several such deliberate echoes between the two catalogs, though the catalogs themselves are of very unequal length (some 26 items across three verses against six in one). Bhārata is Arjuna, descendant of Bharata, addressed here for the first time in the chapter.
#4
L: Hypocrisy, pride, and self-conceit, anger, harshness, and also ignorance — these [come to be] the demonic endowment of one born [to it], O Pārtha.
I: Hypocrisy, pride and self-conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance — these, Pārtha, belong to one born with the demonic endowment.
N: The mirror-list of vices, built exactly like verses 1-3 (bhavanti and sampadam are understood, carried over from verse 3 rather than repeated). darpo 'bhimānaś ca hides two words, darpaḥ (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha) and abhimānaḥ ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-): darpa is 'pride, insolence', abhimāna 'self-conceit, an inflated opinion of oneself'. This is one of the chapter's two places where the received (vulgate) text differs from the BORI critical edition: BORI reads darpo 'timānaś ca, 'pride and excessive pride (atimāna)', in place of the vulgate's darpo 'bhimānaś ca, 'pride and self-conceit (abhimāna)' printed here. Pārtha, 'son of Pṛthā', is again Arjuna.
#5
L: The divine endowment [is] held [to lead] to liberation, the demonic to bondage; do not grieve, you are born, O Pāṇḍava, to the divine endowment.
I: The divine endowment, it is held, leads to liberation; the demonic, to bondage. Do not grieve, Pāṇḍava — you were born with the divine endowment.
N: A single balanced sentence names the stakes of the whole chapter: daivī sampat vimokṣāya, 'the divine endowment [is] for liberation', āsurī nibandhāya, 'the demonic, for bondage' (matā, 'held to be', agreeing with both), the two datives of purpose (vimokṣāya, nibandhāya) set side by side. The second line turns personal: mā śucaḥ, 'do not grieve' (a prohibitive mā with the injunctive śucaḥ, the same construction already used at 18.66's mā śucaḥ; 2.11's aśocyān anvaśocas tvam shares the root √śuc but is a different, ordinary indicative construction, not this prohibitive), reassures Arjuna directly that he himself, daivīm sampadam abhijātaḥ asi, 'you are born to the divine endowment' — answering, in effect, his own despair from chapter 1. Pāṇḍava, 'son of Pāṇḍu', is again Arjuna.
#6
L: Two [are] the creations-of-beings in this world, the divine and the demonic too; the divine has been described at-length — hear from me, O Pārtha, of the demonic.
I: There are two kinds of created beings in this world, the divine and the demonic. I have described the divine at length; now hear from me, Pārtha, about the demonic.
N: This opens the chapter's long central section (through verse 20) on the demonic nature. Bhūta-sargau, 'the two creations/classes of beings', is dual, matching dvau, 'two'. The line hides two separate hiatuses, both left unfused rather than coalescing, in the manner already noted at 15.16's akṣaraḥ eva: loke'smin (loke+asmin, e+a, the a- elided and marked by avagraha) daiva āsura eva ca — daivaḥ loses its visarga before āsuraḥ with the vowels kept apart rather than fusing, and āsuraḥ likewise loses its visarga before eva rather than fusing to āsuraiva. Note that 'the divine has already been described at length' (prokta) refers to nothing earlier in the poem by that name; it is simply Kṛṣṇa's own summary of the divine list just given in verses 1-3, now signaling a matching, and much longer, catalog of the demonic to follow.
#7
L: Right-action and its-cessation, demonic people do not know; nor purity, nor also right-conduct, nor truth is found in them.
I: Demonic people know neither right action nor its cessation; they have no purity, no right conduct, no truthfulness.
N: Pravṛtti and nivṛtti, 'engagement in action' and 'withdrawal from action', are a standing technical pair in the poem (the same terms return, e.g., at 18.30's own pravṛttiṃ ca nivṛttiṃ ca) naming the two poles of moral life: knowing when to act and when not to. Vidur āsurāḥ (viduḥ+āsurāḥ, the visarga after u becoming r before a voiced sound) puts āsurāḥ, 'demonic [people]', in apposition with janāḥ, 'people' — this is the first verse to actually name who is being described, opening a run of purely negative description (verses 7-8 deny them everything) that will run through to the men's own words in verses 13-15.
#8
L: Unreal, without-foundation, they say the world [is], without-a-god; produced-by-mutual-union, [with] desire-as-its-only-cause — what else?
I: They say the world is unreal, baseless, without a god, produced by mere mutual union, with desire as its only cause — what else could it be?
N: This states the demonic cosmology the chapter condemns, directly opposed to the theistic vision of chapters 9-11: the world (jagat) is asatyam, 'unreal', apratiṣṭham, 'without foundation', anīśvaram, 'without a lord, godless'. Aparasparasaṃbhūtam is a well-known crux: aparaspara here is not the privative a- 'not' plus paraspara 'mutual' (which would reverse the sense to 'not produced by mutual [causation]'), but an old form used, already by Śaṅkara's own gloss, as a simple synonym of paraspara, 'one another' — so 'produced by mutual union [of male and female]', with no higher cause. The rhetorical question kim anyat kāma-haitukam, 'what else, caused by desire?', closes the verse: for the demonic view, desire alone explains everything.
#9
L: Holding-fast-to this view, their-selves-lost, of-little-intelligence, they arise, of-fierce-deeds, for the destruction of the world, as-its-enemies.
I: Clinging to this view, their true selves lost, of little understanding, they arise, men of cruel deeds, as enemies of the world, bent on its destruction.
N: Etāṃ dṛṣṭim, 'this view', points back to verse 8's nihilistic cosmology. Two bahuvrīhi compounds describe the men holding it: naṣṭātmānaḥ, 'whose [true] selves are lost' (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha), and alpa-buddhayaḥ, 'of little intelligence'; a third, ugra-karmāṇaḥ, 'of fierce deeds', describes how they act. The clause kṣayāya jagato 'hitāḥ shares one genitive, jagataḥ, between two constructions — 'for the destruction of the world' and 'as enemies of the world' — a common economy in Sanskrit where a single case-form serves two phrases at once.
#10
L: Given-over-to insatiable desire, filled-with-hypocrisy-pride-and-arrogance, through delusion holding-to false-notions, they act, their-observances-impure.
I: Given over to desire that can never be satisfied, filled with hypocrisy, pride and arrogance, clinging through delusion to false notions, they act with their resolves impure.
N: The whole second half-line of this verse — mohād gṛhītvāsadgrāhān pravartante 'śucivratāḥ — is written as a single unbroken Devanagari token, the densest sandhi run in the chapter; reading it means finding five separate words inside it: mohāt (abl., 'through delusion'; -t+g-→-d g-), gṛhītvā ('having adopted'; +a-→ā, vowel fusion), asad-grāhān ('false notions', -t+g-→-d g-, acc. pl., object of gṛhītvā), pravartante ('they act'), and aśuci-vratāḥ ('whose observances are impure', -e+a-→-e' with avagraha). Kāmam duṣpūram āśritya, 'given over to desire hard to fill/insatiable', and dambha-māna-mada-anvitāḥ, 'filled with hypocrisy, pride and arrogance', complete the first line's description.
#11
L: Beset-by immeasurable anxiety, ending-only-in-death, holding-sense-enjoyment-as-the-highest-goal, certain [that] 'this-much [is all],'
I: Beset by anxiety beyond measure, ending only in death, holding sense-enjoyment as life's highest goal, sure that this is all there is —
N: This verse continues the sentence into verse 12 (there is no finite verb here; īhante, 'they strive', in verse 12 carries the whole description). Cintām aparimeyāṃ pralayāntām upāśritāḥ, 'beset by immeasurable anxiety ending [only] in death' (pralaya-antām, 'having death as its end'), and kāmopabhogaparamāḥ, 'holding the gratification of desire as the highest [goal]' (bahuvrīhi), lead into a quoted thought marked by iti: etāvad iti niścitāḥ, 'certain that "this is all [there is]"' — the first of several places in this section where the demonic men's own reasoning is quoted directly, anticipating the extended monologue of verses 13-15.
#12
L: Bound by hundreds-of-ties-of-hope, given-over-to desire-and-anger, they strive, for-the-sake-of-gratifying-desire, by unjust-means, [to amass] hoards-of-wealth.
I: Bound by hundreds of chains of hope, given over to desire and anger, they strive by unjust means to amass wealth for the sake of gratifying their desires.
N: Āśā-pāśa-śataiḥ baddhāḥ, 'bound by hundreds of ties of hope' (āśā, 'hope, expectation', pictured as a rope binding them), and kāma-krodha-parāyaṇāḥ, 'given over to desire and anger' (a phrase that will recur, in the singular, at verse 21's naming of desire and anger among the three gates of hell), set up the verse's one finite verb, īhante, 'they strive'. The final compound, kāma-bhoga-artham anyāyena artha-sañcayān, 'for the sake of gratifying desire, by unjust means, hoards of wealth', packs the whole point of their striving into a single phrase: acquisition, by any means, for the sake of appetite.
#13
L: 'This today by-me has-been-gained; this desire I-shall-attain [next]; this exists, and this wealth too shall further be mine.'
I: 'This I have gained today; this desire I shall fulfill next. This is mine, and this wealth too will be mine besides.'
N: Verses 13-15 quote the demonic man's inner monologue directly, closed by iti at the end of verse 15 (modiṣya iti) — grammatically all of it is what he is imagined saying to himself. This is the second of the chapter's two places where the vulgate differs from BORI: the vulgate reads labdham imaṃ prāpsye, 'this [imam, masculine, agreeing with manoratham] I shall attain', which is what is printed and read here; BORI reads labdham idaṃ prāpsye, with the neuter idam in its place. Manoratham, literally 'mind's chariot', is the ordinary Sanskrit word for 'a wish, a fancy, a desire' — the thing this man is forever chasing next.
#14
L: 'That enemy has-been-slain by-me, and I-shall-slay others too; I [am] the lord, I [am] the enjoyer, I [am] accomplished, powerful, happy;'
I: 'That enemy I have killed, and I will kill others too. I am the lord, I am the one who enjoys, I am accomplished, powerful, and happy.'
N: The monologue continues with a string of first-person boasts, aham repeated three times — once eliding into īśvaraḥ (īśvaro'ham, -aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha), immediately doubled before bhogī (aham aham, the second simply following the first, -m unaffected before the vowel), and once more eliding into siddhaḥ (siddho'ham, -aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha): 'I am the lord [īśvaraḥ], I am the enjoyer [bhogī], I am accomplished [siddhaḥ], powerful, happy.' The self-glorifying anaphora is the point — each clause restates the same swollen 'I' in a new guise, exactly the ahaṃkāra, 'egotism', that verse 18 will name outright.
#15
L: 'I [am] wealthy and well-born; who else is there like me? I-shall-sacrifice, I-shall-give, I-shall-rejoice' — thus, deluded-by-ignorance,
I: 'I am rich and well-born — who else is there like me? I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, I shall enjoy myself' — so they think, deluded by ignorance,
N: The monologue closes here, marked by iti: modiṣya iti, 'thus [thinking], "I shall rejoice."' Modiṣye, the plain future middle 'I shall rejoice', shows an idiosyncratic sandhi before this particular iti, its ātmanepada -e ending simply becoming -a (modiṣye+iti→modiṣya iti) rather than the usual coalescence or retained hiatus seen elsewhere in the chapter — an oddity of this verb-ending before iti, reproduced here exactly as transmitted. Ajñāna-vimohitāḥ, 'deluded by ignorance', is the narrator's own verdict, stepping back from the quoted boast to name it for what it is, and opening directly into verse 16's account of where such delusion leads.
#16
L: Bewildered-by-manifold-thoughts, entangled-in-the-net-of-delusion, addicted to the gratification-of-desire, they fall into a foul hell.
I: Confused by countless thoughts, caught in the net of delusion, addicted to sense-gratification, they fall into a foul hell.
N: Two bahuvrīhi compounds describe the fate of the men whose monologue just closed: aneka-citta-vibhrāntāḥ, 'bewildered by manifold (an-eka, 'not-one') thoughts', and moha-jāla-samāvṛtāḥ, 'entangled in the net of delusion'. Prasaktāḥ kāma-bhogeṣu, 'addicted to the gratification of desire', gives the one finite verb of the verse, patanti, its subject: they fall, patanti, narake 'śucau, 'into a foul hell' (-e+a-→-e' with avagraha) — the first of two consequences (this and verse 19-20's rebirth in demonic wombs) that the chapter draws from the character just described.
#17
L: Self-conceited, stubborn, filled-with-the-pride-and-arrogance-of-wealth, they sacrifice, with-sacrifices-in-name-only, with hypocrisy, not-according-to-rule.
I: Self-important and stubborn, puffed up with the pride of wealth, they perform sacrifices that are sacrifices in name only, out of hypocrisy, without regard for the proper rites.
N: A new group of demonic traits, centered on false religion: ātma-saṃbhāvitāḥ, 'self-esteeming, self-conceited', and stabdhāḥ, 'stubborn, arrogant' (its visarga dropping before the voiced dh- that follows, as elsewhere in this chapter's -āḥ endings), dhana-māna-mada-anvitāḥ, 'filled with the pride and arrogance of wealth'. Such men yajante nāma-yajñais, 'sacrifice with name-sacrifices' — rites that are sacrifices in name only — dambhena avidhi-pūrvakam, 'with hypocrisy, not according to [scriptural] rule (vidhi)' — the word vidhi returning at the chapter's very end, in verse 24's śāstra-vidhi, 'the injunction of scripture', which these men flout in advance.
#18
L: Given-over-to egotism, force, pride, desire, and anger, hating me in the bodies of self and others, malicious —
I: Given over to egotism, violence, pride, desire and anger, they hate me as I dwell in their own bodies and in others', and are malicious besides —
N: A list of five things such men are saṃśritāḥ, 'given over to' — ahaṃkāram, balam, darpam, kāmam, krodham, 'egotism, force, pride, desire, anger' — leads to the verse's real charge: mām ātma-para-deheṣu pradviṣantaḥ, 'hating me in the bodies of self and others'. The 'me' is Kṛṣṇa as the indwelling self present in every body, the same presence taught at length in chapter 13 (the kṣetrajña) and named directly at 6.29's sarva-bhūta-stham ātmānam — so that hatred directed at any being is, in the poem's logic, hatred of Kṛṣṇa himself. Abhyasūyakāḥ, 'malicious, fault-finding', closes the list.
#19
L: Those hating [me], cruel, basest-of-men — evil — I hurl, continually, in the rounds-of-rebirth, into demonic wombs alone.
I: Those hateful, cruel, and vilest of men, ever wicked, I continually hurl down, through the cycle of rebirth, into demonic wombs alone.
N: Kṛṣṇa now states the consequence directly, in the first person: tān aham ... kṣipāmi, 'those men I hurl down'. Krūrān, 'cruel' (agreeing with tān, 'those'), is a correction: the source text here restores क्रूरान् (long ū), correcting a Wikisource misprint क्रुरान् (short u), and matches the BORI reading krūrān; the correction is adopted throughout this reading and translation, as it must be named here per the pipeline's editorial rule. Saṃsāreṣu, 'in the rounds of rebirth', names the whole sphere across which the hurling takes place, not a single destination; āsurīṣv eva yoniṣu, 'into demonic wombs alone', with eva restrictively emphasizing that no other kind of rebirth awaits them.
#20
L: Fallen into a demonic womb, deluded, birth after birth, not-attaining me at all, O Kaunteya, they go, thence, to the lowest state.
I: Fallen into a demonic womb, deluded from birth to birth, never reaching me, Kaunteya, they sink at last to the lowest state.
N: This closes the long central section (verses 6-20) on the demonic nature. Janmani janmani, 'in birth, in birth', doubles a single locative to mean 'birth after birth', a common Sanskrit device for expressing repetition (compare pratyakṣam pratyakṣam and similar doublings elsewhere in the epics). Mām aprāpyaiva, 'without ever attaining me' (aprāpya+eva→aprāpyaiva, a+e→ai), states in the negative what verse 18's hatred already implied: cut off from Kṛṣṇa lifetime after lifetime, they sink, yānti, to adhamāṃ gatim, 'the lowest state' — the grim endpoint of the chapter's central portrait. Kaunteya, 'son of Kuntī', is again Arjuna.
#21
L: Threefold [is] this gate of hell, destructive-of-the-self — desire, and anger, and likewise greed; therefore one-should-abandon this triad.
I: This gate of hell has three parts, and it destroys the self: desire, anger, and greed. One should therefore give up all three.
N: The chapter turns to its closing counsel (verses 21-22). Narakasya idam dvāram, 'this gate of hell' (narakasya+idam→narakasyedam, a+i→e), trividham, 'threefold', is named outright: kāmaḥ krodhas tathā lobhaḥ, 'desire, anger, and likewise greed' — the first two already named repeatedly through the chapter (verses 4, 8, 10, 12, 18), the third, lobha, 'greed', introduced here for the first time, completing the set. Ātmanaḥ nāśanam, 'destructive of the self', names the stakes directly: these three do not merely lead to hell, they annihilate the self that falls into them.
#22
L: Freed from these three dark-gates, O Kaunteya, a man does what-is-good for himself; thence he goes to the highest goal.
I: A man who is freed from these three dark gates, Kaunteya, does what is best for himself, and so reaches the highest goal.
N: This answers verse 21's warning with its positive counterpart: etaiḥ ... tamo-dvāraiḥ tribhiḥ vimuktaḥ naraḥ, 'a man freed from these three dark gates' (tamo-dvāraiḥ, 'gates of darkness', renaming verse 21's triad with the word tamas, the same guṇa of darkness and inertia described at length in chapter 14), ācarati ātmanaḥ śreyaḥ, 'does what is good for himself', and so yāti parāṃ gatim, 'goes to the highest goal' — the same phrase, parāṃ gatim, that verse 23 will deny to the man who ignores scripture, and verse 20 denied, in its low form (adhamāṃ gatim), to the demonic.
#23
L: Who, having-abandoned the injunction-of-scripture, acts according-to-mere-desire — he attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal.
I: Whoever casts aside the injunctions of scripture and acts on mere desire attains neither success, nor happiness, nor the highest goal.
N: A relative-correlative sentence (yaḥ ... sa, 'who ... he') states the chapter's practical conclusion: whoever śāstra-vidhim utsṛjya, 'having abandoned the injunction of scripture', vartate kāma-kārataḥ, 'acts according to mere desire, willfully' (kāma-kāra, 'acting from desire', with the adverbial suffix -tas), na sa siddhim avāpnoti, na sukhaṃ na parāṃ gatim, 'attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal' — a triple negation that denies him everything the chapter has held out as the reward of the divine endowment.
#24
L: Therefore scripture [is] the authority for-you in-determining-what-should-and-should-not-be-done; having-known what-is-declared-by-the-ordinance-of-scripture, you-ought to-act here.
I: Scripture, therefore, is your authority in deciding what should and should not be done. Knowing what the ordinance of scripture declares, you should act accordingly in this world.
N: The chapter's closing verse draws the moral in general terms, anticipating the poem's own return to this same argument at 18.5-6, and its final closing counsel at 18.63-66: tasmāt śāstraṃ pramāṇaṃ te, 'therefore scripture is your authority' (tasmāt+śāstram→tasmācchāstram, -t+ś-→-c ch-), kāryākāryavyavasthitau, 'in determining what should and should not be done' (kārya, 'what is to be done', and its negation a-kārya). The final construction, jñātvā ... kartum ihārhasi, 'having known ..., you ought to act here [in this world]', pairs a gerund of knowing with an infinitive-plus-'ought' of doing — knowledge of the rule is only the first step; acting on it is the point.
